I am 76 years old, and my bones ache when the weather turns. I have farmed these 6.5 mu in Quzhou for 50 years, since I was a young bride. My husband and I are the only ones left at home, so I cannot take risks or do heavy lifting. I know this soil like my own hands—it is loamy but tired, and the well water is my lifeline.

I will put 5 mu into the wheat-maize rotation that has never failed me. Wheat is my winter crop; I will buy improved seed from the township store, rotary till after the maize stubble is cleared, and sow in mid-October. I will put down compound fertilizer and urea—about 16 jin of nitrogen per mu, split between planting and green-up. I will irrigate three times: the wintering water before freeze-up, once at jointing when the spring winds blow, and once at heading. I will spray herbicide once and insecticide once; that is enough if you watch the fields every day.

After the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant hybrid maize seed directly into the stubble without tilling—no-tillage saves me time and precious soil moisture during the hot summer. I will side-dress nitrogen when the plants reach my knee, irrigate twice at jointing and filling if the sky does not give rain, and spray twice for weeds and corn borer. 

The remaining 1.5 mu I keep in cotton because the price has been steady and I know how to read the bollworm. But cotton is cruel on an old woman's back. I will rotary till in late April, plant improved cotton seed, and apply compound fertilizer as a base. I must irrigate three times—seedling, flowering, and boll stage—and spray five times when the pests appear. I expect to hire village women to help pick in autumn, or my niece might come.

I keep my fertilizer moderate because fertilizer costs have risen and my land responds well to what I give it. I use the well carefully because pumping costs electricity. I do not chase the highest possible yield; I chase a yield I can achieve with my two old hands and a little hired help, without losing money.
